title: WPMS/143/2010 of BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICALS LIMITED Vs SH. MAHMOOD KHAN

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT
NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 143 of 2010
Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited ... Petitioner
Versus
Sh. Mahmood Khan ... Respondent
Mr. V.K. Kohli, Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr.
I.P. Kohli, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Senior Advocate, for the
respondent.

21.11.2023
Hon'ble Manoj Kumar Tiwari, A.C.J.
Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited, a
Public Sector undertaking of the Central
Government (hereinafter referred to as 'BHEL')
has filed this writ petition challenging the
judgment dated 14.12.2009 rendered by
Additional District Judge/FTC-IV, Haridwar in
Miscellaneous Appeal No. 73 of 2008
(Mahmood Khan v. BHEL). By the impugned
judgment, learned Additional District Judge has
set aside the eviction order passed against the
respondent by Estate Officer under the
provisions of Public Premises (Eviction of
Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971.
2. A notice under Section 4 of Public
Premises (Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants)
Act, 1971 (for short "Public Premises Act,
1971") was issued to the respondent by Estate
Officer, BHEL Township, Ranipur, Haridwar
stating that respondent has illegally occupied

2
land, admeasuring 1 Bigha 7 Biswas packa,
belonging to BHEL comprised in Khasra No.32
in Village Jamalpur Khurd, near Bahadrabad
Barrier No.6 of BHEL, Tehsil & District
Haridwar. In his reply to the notice,
respondent relied on a sale deed dated
30.08.1996 allegedly executed in his favour by
one Suresh Chand S/o Gugal Chand as power
of attorney holder of Achpal Singh S/o Meer
Singh. The Estate Officer for BHEL premises
passed an eviction order against the
respondent, on 26.09.1998, by holding that
respondent could not produce any evidence in
support of his claim regarding his ownership or
title of his predecessor-in-interest, from whom
he allegedly purchased the land in question.
The Estate Officer further held that the land in
question was acquired by BHEL in the year
1962 and possession thereof was also handed
over by the State Government to BHEL,
therefore, in view of provision contained in
Section 16 of Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the
land stands vested in BHEL, free from all
encumbrances.
3. The eviction order dated 26.09.1998
was challenged by respondent in a Appeal filed
under Section 9 of the Public Premises Act,
1971, which was registered as Misc. Appeal
No.112 of 1998. Learned District Judge,
Haridwar allowed the Appeal and remanded
the matter back to Estate Officer with direction
to decide the matter afresh, after giving
opportunity to the respondent to produce

3
evidence in support of his claim for title and
also to cross-examine BHEL's witnesses. Upon
remand of the matter, respondent filed written
statement before the Estate Officer and both
the parties adduced evidence. The Estate
Officer, again, passed an eviction order against
the respondent, on 27.11.2008.
4. From the eviction order dated
27.11.2008, it is revealed that the Estate
Officer had framed following four issues:
"(i) Whether the possession of O.P. on
the disputed land - khasra no. 32 is
unauthorized and whether he is liable to
be evicted?
(ii) Whether the proceedings in
pursuance of notice are not
maintainable?
(iii) Whether the case is barred by
section 10 CPC?
(iv) Whether the disputed land has
been purchased by O.P. and this court
has no jurisdiction to hear the dispute?"
5. On issue no.1, Estate Officer
returned a finding that the land in question
was acquired for BHEL by the State
Government and possession thereof was
handed over to BHEL, on 17.03.1962,
therefore, the land belongs to BHEL and
respondent's claim of title, based on a sale
deed executed in the year 1996, cannot be
accepted. Based on the statement made by
respondent and his witness Shamim Ahmed
that respondent's possession dates back to
1990, Estate Officer returned a finding that
respondent had occupied BHEL land with
malafide intention and, subsequently, he

4
managed to get a sale deed executed in his
favour to give legal colour to his unauthorized
occupation over BHEL land.
6. Similarly, issue no.2 was decided in
favour of petitioner by holding that the notice
issued to respondent is valid and proceedings
issued pursuant to the said notice are
maintainable. Issue no.3 was also decided in
favour of BHEL and it was held that withdrawal
of injunction suit by BHEL, in which respondent
was also a party, will not bar eviction
proceedings under Public Premises Act, 1971.
7. Issue no.4 was also decided against
the respondent by holding that since land
comprised in Khasra No.32 was acquired for
BHEL and BHEL has become absolute owner of
the said land, therefore, any sale deed
executed in respect of land comprised in
Khasra No.32, after its acquisition by BHEL, is
nullity in the eyes of law, therefore, the Estate
Officer has jurisdiction to hear & decide the
matter.
8. Feeling aggrieved by the eviction
order dated 27.11.2008 passed by Estate
Officer, respondent again filed Misc. Appeal
No.73 of 2008 before learned District Judge,
Haridwar. The memo of Misc. Appeal No.73 of
2008 is enclosed as Annexure No.17 to the writ
petition. The eviction order was challenged by
the respondent on the ground that area of
Khasra No.32 is 11 Bigha 19 Biswa 10 Biswansi

5
(2.544 hectare), out of which, only 0.468
hectare belongs to BHEL and the land,
regarding which notice was given to the
respondent, is not identifiable based on the
description of the land given in the notice. It
was further contended that BHEL had filed a
suit for permanent injunction, in which it had
claimed possession over entire Khasra No.32,
but Estate Officer has not considered the said
aspect in the impugned order.
9. The Misc. Appeal No.73 of 2008 filed
by the respondent was allowed by learned
Additional District Judge/ F.T.C.-IV, Haridwar
vide judgment dated 14.12.2009. BHEL has
filed this writ petition challenging the judgment
dated 14.12.2009 rendered by learned
Appellate Court.
10. Heard learned counsel for the parties
and perused the record. Learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the petitioner submits
that learned Appellate Court wrongly shifted
the burden of proof upon petitioner (BHEL)
that it is the owner of the premises in
question. Attention of this Court is drawn to
the points for determination, formulated by the
Appellate Court, which are extracted below:
"(i) Whether the applicant/ respondent
is owner of the premises and has a right
to evict the opposite party/appellant
from it.
(ii) Whether the notice issued by the
applicant/respondent is valid.
(iii) Whether the applicant/ respondent
waived the notice.

6
(iv) Whether the learned Estate Officer
followed due procedure while passing
eviction order against the opposite
party/appellant.
(v) Relief."
11. Mr. V.K. Kohli, learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the petitioner contends
that as there was sufficient material on record
that the land in question, which is part of
Khasra No.32, was acquired by BHEL in the
year 1962 and the Estate Officer has dealt with
the said issue in the eviction order, therefore,
point no. 1 formulated for determination by the
Appellate Court was not proper. He further
contended that in the grounds of Appeal,
respondent himself admitted that Khasra
No.32 was acquired for BHEL, therefore, the
burden to prove its title could not have been
shifted to BHEL. Learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioner further submits that respondent
has claimed title over the land in question
based on a sale deed executed by one Suresh
Chand as power of attorney holder of Achpal
Singh, however, in the sale deed, there is no
recital how Achpal Singh became owner of the
land in question. He further submitted that
Achpal Singh did not have any title in respect
of land, which was acquired by BHEL in 1962,
therefore, the sale deed relied by the
respondent is a nullity. He further contended
that no material was brought on record by the
respondent in support of his contention that
Achpal Singh was owner of the land, and
further that Achpal Singh in a Civil Suit had
deposed before the Court that he does not

7
have any right on interest over land comprised
in Khasra No. 32.
12. Per contra, Mr. Arvind Vashistha,
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
respondent submitted that area of Khasra No.
32 is 11 Bigha 19 Biswa 10 Biswansi (2.544
hectare) and only a part thereof was acquired
by BHEL in the year 1962 and the sale deed
executed in favour of respondent was in
respect of land other than the land which was
acquired by BHEL, therefore, the question of
title formulated by the Appellate Court was
germane for deciding the Appeal.
13. This Court finds substance in the
submission made by learned Senior Counsel
for the petitioner. Public Premises (Eviction of
Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971 was
enacted with a view to provide speedy remedy
for eviction of unauthorized occupants of public
premises to the Central Government or
Companies/Statutory Corporations owned or
controlled by the Central Government. From
the scheme of the Act, it is apparent that the
question of title cannot be gone into in the
proceedings under the said Act. The Act
provides that whenever a person is found in
unauthorized occupation over public premises,
then a notice has to be given to him under
Section 4 of the Act asking him to show cause
as to why an order of eviction be not passed
against him. Thus, the initial burden is upon
the person in authorized occupation to show

8
the authority under which he is occupying the
public premises. Since respondent had
asserted his title by relying upon a sale deed,
therefore, learned Estate Officer had
formulated four points for determination, which
are extracted in para 4 of this judgment. The
issues so framed by the Estate Officer are in
line with the scheme of Public Premises
(Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants) Act,
1971. However, learned Appellate Authority
went astray in shifting the burden of proof
upon BHEL (petitioner), as is revealed by the
points formulated for determination by the
Appellate Authority. Points for determination
formulated by the Appellate Authority are also
reproduced in para 6 of this judgment.
14. Public Premises (Eviction of
Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971 is a special
statute which prescribes different procedure
for evicting unauthorized occupants from public
premises and carves out an exception from the
normal procedure. This Act prescribes a
summary procedure, which does not elaborate
the procedural aspects and is a departure from
the normal procedure. Section 4 and 5 of the
said Act lay down the procedure which has to
be followed before passing an order of eviction
against any person. For ready reference,
Section 4 and 5 are reproduced below:
"4. Issue of notice to show cause
against order of eviction.-

9
(1) If the estate officer has information
that any person is in unauthorised
occupation of any public premises and
that he should be evicted, the estate
officer shall issue in the manner
hereinafter provided a notice in writing
within seven working days from the date
of receipt of the information regarding
the unauthorised occupation calling
upon the person concerned to show
cause why an order of eviction should
not be made.
(1A) If the estate officer knows or has
reasons to believe that any person is in
unauthorized occupation of the public
premises, then, without prejudice to the
provisions of sub-section (1), he shall
forthwith issue a notice in writing calling
upon the person concerned to show
cause why an order of eviction should
not be made.
(1B) Any delay in issuing a notice
referred to in sub-sections (1) and (1A)
shall not vitiate the proceedings under
this Act.
(2) The notice shall-
(a) specify the grounds on which the
order of eviction is proposed to be
made; and
(b) require all persons concerned, that is
to say, all persons who are, or may be,
in occupation of, or claim interest in, the
public premises,-
(i) to show cause, if any, against the
proposed order on or before such date
as is specified in the notice, being a date
not later than seven days from the date
of issue thereof; and
(ii) to appear before the estate officer
on the date specified in the notice along
with the evidence which they intend to
produce in support of the cause shown,
and also for personal hearing, if such
hearing is desired.
(3) The estate officer shall cause the
notice to be served by having it affixed
on the outer door or some other
conspicuous part of the public premises,
and in such other manner as may be
prescribed, whereupon the notice shall

10
be deemed to have been duly given to
all persons concerned.
5. Eviction of unauthorised
occupants.-
(1) If, after considering the cause, if
any, shown by any person in pursuance
of a notice under section 4 and any
evidence produced by him in support of
the same and after personal hearing, if
any, given under sub-clause (ii) of
clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section
4, the estate officer is satisfied that the
public premises are in unauthorised
occupation, the estate officer shall make
an order of eviction, for reasons to be
recorded therein, directing that the
public premises shall be vacated, on
such date as may be specified in the
order but not later than fifteen days
from the date of order, by all persons
who may be in occupation thereof or
any part thereof, and cause a copy of
the order to be affixed on the outer door
or some other conspicuous part of the
public premises:
Provided that every order under
this sub-section shall be made by the
estate officer as expeditiously as
possible and all endeavour shall be
made by him to issue the order within
fifteen days of the date specified in the
notice under sub-section (1) or sub-section (1A), as the case may be, of
section 4.
(2) If any person refuses or fails to
comply with the order of eviction on or
before the date specified in the said
order or within fifteen days of the date
of its publication under sub-section (1),
whichever is later, the estate officer or
any other officer duly authorised by the
estate officer in this behalf may, after
the date so specified or after the expiry
of the period aforesaid, whichever is
later, evict that person from, and take
possession of, the public premises and
may, for that purpose, use such force as
may be necessary:
Provided that if the estate officer is
satisfied, for reasons to be recorded in
writing, that there exists any compelling

11
reason which prevents the person from
vacating the premises within fifteen
days, the estate officer may grant
another fifteen days from the date of
expiry of the order under sub-section
(1) to the person to vacate the
premises."
15. In the case of Kanpur Development
Authority, Kanpur v. Banwari Lal & Others,
reported in (1998) 1 ARC 611, while dealing
with provisions under Section 4 and 5 of the
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorized
Occupants) Act, 1971, Hon'ble Allahabad High
Court has observed as under:
"A perusal of the said section makes it
clear that as soon as the prescribed
authority is of the opinion that any
person is in unauthorised occupation of
the public premises and that he should
be evicted, notice in writing is to be
issued by him calling upon such persons
to show cause why eviction should not
be made. Thus when the prescribed
authority is of the opinion, he issues
notice requiring the person concerned
to show cause why order of eviction
should not be made. The notice will
specify the grounds for the proposed
eviction. The procedure prescribed,
therefore, shows that it is for the
person concerned who has to show
cause as to why order of eviction should
not be made against him. The moment
notice is issued, it is open to the person
on whom burden lies to prove that such
order of eviction should not be made.
5. Similarly, Section 5 provides that
after considering the cause shown by
such person pursuant to such notice or
any evidence that such person may
produce in support of the cause shown
by him and if the prescribed authority is
satisfied that the person occupying the
public premises is unauthorised then
the order of eviction is to be made.
Thus Section 5 also provides that cause
is to be shown by the person concerned

12
and the evidence has to be given by
him to prove that he is not in
unauthorised occupation of any public
premises. Therefore, the question of
burden as has been discussed in the
impugned order, appears to be wholly
misconceived and contrary to the
provisions of Sections 4 and 5 of the
said Act.
6. Since the person concerned in the
present case was claiming that their
houses were not situated in plots No.
539 and 543, it was for them to show
by production of sufficient plan or map
as to on which plots their houses were
situated. It does not appear from the
material on record that the said persons
had claimed that their houses were
situated at a particular plot other than
plots No. 539 and 543. The only claim
that has been made is to the effect that
their houses were not constructed
within the area of plots Nos. 539 and
543. In absence of any specific
pleadings, simply on the assertion that
their houses were not situated within
plots No. 539 and 543, the burden
could never be shifted on the petitioner
to prove that their houses were not
situated within plots No. 539 and 543.
Therefore, it was incumbent on the
person concerned to show cause that
their houses were not situated within
plots No. 539 and 543 particularly when
ownership of plots No. 539 and 543 of
the petitioner was not disputed."
16. A Division Bench of Hon'ble Delhi High
Court, in the case of Union of India v. S.M.
Aggarwal & 31 Ors. (Civil Writ Petition No. 4123
of 1994), held as follows:
"(11) The procedure followed by the
learned Additional District Judge was
not what is contemplated by the Act.
His order has resulted in miscarriage of
justice and is against the provisions of
law. It is not for the Central
Government to lead evidence and to
subject its witnesses to cross-

13
examination, and that too without the
shopkeepers having shown any cause
as to why the order of eviction should
not be made against them. We,
therefore, find that the impugned order
of the Additional District Judge is wholly
without jurisdiction and has to be set
aside. We order accordingly. We,
therefore, send the matter back to the
learned Additional District Judge to
decide the appeals pending before him
in accordance with the provisions of the
Act. In the circumstances of the present
case, we direct the District Judge to
assign these appeals to some other
Additional District Judge for disposal.
The parties shall appear before the
District Judge on 1 May 1995 for the
purpose. Petition is allowed with costs.
Counsel fee Rs.2,000."
17. Learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the petitioner further submitted that points
for determination formulated by the Appellate
Court are beyond the pleadings made by the
respondent, as he has not taken any such plea
either in his pleading before the Estate Officer
nor in his grounds of Appeal. He further
submitted that although respondent contended
that he purchased the land from Achpal Singh
through his attorney, however, neither any
evidence was led as to how Achpal Singh
became owner of the land nor Achpal Singh
was examined as witness. He has drawn
attention of this Court to the cross-examination of Mr. Achpal Singh in some other
case, which is enclosed as Annexure No.15
(page 100 to the writ petition), where Achpal
Singh has stated that he does not know Suresh
Chand (who executed sale deed as his
attorney). Achpal Singh further stated that

14
Khasra No.32 does not belong to him and the
sale deed, if any, executed by Suresh Chand
on his behalf to the respondent, is not
acceptable to him.
18. This Court finds substance in the
contention raised on behalf of the petitioner.
The approach adopted by learned Appellate
Court, while deciding Misc. Appeal No.73 of
2008, is contrary to the scheme of the Act.
BHEL had initiated eviction proceedings against
the respondent by invoking proceedings of
Public Premises Act, 1971, therefore, it was
incumbent upon the respondent to prove that
he is not in unauthorized occupation over any
public premises. The Estate Officer had
considered and discussed the question of title
of BHEL and held that land in question was
acquired by invoking provisions of Land
Acquisition Act, 1894. Learned Appellate Court,
however, shifted the burden of proving its title
upon the petitioner. Similarly, the points for
determination formulated by the Appellate
Court, specifically point nos.1, 3 & 4, are
beyond the pleadings made by respondent,
thus, were not necessary. Thus, the impugned
judgment rendered by learned Additional
District Judge cannot be sustained in the eyes
of law.
19. Accordingly, the writ petition is
allowed and the order dated 14.12.2009
passed by learned Additional District Judge/
F.T.C.-IV, Haridwar is set aside. The matter is

15
remanded back to the Appellate Court for
decision afresh. Miscellaneous Civil Appeal No.
73 of 2008 is restored to the file of District &
Sessions Judge, Haridwar, who may himself
decide the Appeal or assign it for disposal to
Additional District Judge. This Court hopes &
expects that the said Appeal shall be decided
as early as possible, preferably within nine
months, without being influenced by any
observation made by this Court touching the
merits of the case.
 (Manoj Kumar Tiwari, A.C.J.)
Pr
